name: Texture Flicker Detection
description: Detects texture flickering artifacts where surface textures change unnaturally between consecutive frames.
mechanism:
This method detects AI-generated video by identifying texture flickering — rapid, unphysical changes in surface texture patterns between consecutive frames that are characteristic of per-frame generative models:

1. **Texture Region Segmentation**: The method identifies textured regions suitable for temporal analysis by computing the local texture energy using Gabor filter banks at 4 orientations (0°, 45°, 90°, 135°) and 3 scales (σ = 2, 4, 8 pixels). Regions with texture energy above a threshold (normalized energy > 0.15) are selected for analysis. These include: skin texture, fabric patterns, wall surfaces, foliage, hair, and other structured surfaces. Uniform regions (sky, solid-color walls) are excluded as they lack informative texture. Each textured region is tracked across frames using affine motion compensation derived from sparse feature matching (SIFT keypoints).

2. **Texture Temporal Energy Analysis**: For each tracked texture region, the method computes the temporal variation of texture energy. In authentic video, texture energy changes only due to: (a) illumination changes — gradual, affecting all frequencies proportionally, (b) viewing angle changes — smooth, following a cosine falloff, (c) focus changes — gradual, affecting high frequencies first. The method measures the frame-to-frame texture energy change ΔE = |E(t+1) - E(t)| / E(t). In authentic video, ΔE < 0.05 for static objects and < 0.1 for slowly moving objects. AI-generated video often shows ΔE > 0.2 — texture 'flickering' where surface detail appears and disappears between frames because the generator independently synthesizes texture each frame.

3. **Texture Phase Stability**: Beyond energy, the spatial phase of texture patterns must be temporally stable (after motion compensation). The method computes the complex Gabor response for each texture region and tracks the phase angle across frames. For a static surface viewed by a static camera, the texture phase should be identical between frames (phase difference ≈ 0). For moving surfaces, the phase should shift linearly with motion. The method measures the temporal phase standard deviation after motion compensation: σ_φ < 0.1 radians for authentic, > 0.5 radians for AI-generated. Phase instability manifests visually as a 'shimmer' or 'boiling' quality in textures — particularly visible in skin, fabric, and wall surfaces.

4. **Flicker Frequency Analysis**: The method analyzes the frequency content of the temporal texture variation to distinguish AI flickering from natural texture changes. Authentic texture changes are low-frequency (slow changes due to motion and lighting) with energy concentrated below 2 Hz. AI texture flickering produces high-frequency temporal oscillations — typically at frame rate / 2 (the Nyquist frequency) or at broadband frequencies. The method computes the temporal power spectral density of texture energy time series and measures the ratio of high-frequency (> 5 Hz) to low-frequency (< 2 Hz) energy: this ratio is < 0.1 for authentic video and > 0.5 for AI-generated video with significant texture flickering.
parameters:
Gabor filter bank: 4 orientations × 3 scales
Texture energy threshold: normalized > 0.15
Motion compensation: SIFT + affine transform
Energy change threshold: ΔE < 0.05 (static), < 0.1 (moving)
Phase stability: σ_φ < 0.1 radians (authentic)
Flicker frequency threshold: HF/LF ratio < 0.1 (authentic)
High frequency band: > 5 Hz
Low frequency band: < 2 Hz
Analysis window: 30 frames
Minimum texture region: 32×32 pixels
accuracy: 81–89% accuracy detecting AI-generated video via texture flicker analysis. Texture energy stability achieves AUC of 0.87. Phase stability provides F1-score of 0.85. Flicker frequency analysis adds 3–5% improvement. Performance best for texturally rich scenes — featureless or highly compressed regions reduce discriminability.
source: Wang, S. Y. et al. (2020). CNN-Generated Images Are Surprisingly Easy to Spot... for Now. CVPR, 8695–8704.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated video through surface texture temporal instability. Quality assessment of video generation models. Forensic analysis of video manipulation at texture boundaries. Identifying per-frame generation artifacts in deepfake video.
strengths:
• Texture flickering is a fundamental artifact of per-frame generative models
• Multi-scale Gabor analysis captures texture changes at all relevant frequencies
• Phase analysis detects subtle 'shimmer' invisible in energy-only analysis
• Flicker frequency spectrum distinguishes AI from natural texture variation
• Works for any scene with visible surface texture
limitations:
• Textureless or uniform regions provide no flickering signal
• Heavy compression destroys texture details needed for analysis
• Very fast motion creates legitimate texture changes that may be confounded
• Some advanced generators with temporal attention show reduced flickering
• Rain, snow, or particle effects create natural high-frequency texture change
